# EP-264

## Problem Statement
Let $a_n$ be a sequence of positive integers such that for every bounded sequence of integers $b_n$ (with $a_n+b_n\neq 0$ and $b_n\neq 0$ for all $n$) the sum\[\sum \frac{1}{a_n+b_n}\]is irrational. Are $a_n=2^n$ or $a_n=n!$ examples of such a sequence?

## Site Remarks
A possible definition of an 'irrationality sequence' (see also [262] and [263]). One example is $a_n=2^{2^n}$. In \cite{ErGr80} they also ask whether such a sequence can have polynomial growth, but Erd\H{o}s later retracted this in \cite{Er88c}, claiming 'It is not hard to show that it cannot increase slower than exponentially'.

Kova\v{c} and Tao \cite{KoTa24} have proved that $2^n$ is not such an irrationality sequence. More generally, they prove that any strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that $\sum\frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and\[\liminf \left(a_n^2\sum_{k>n}\frac{1}{a_k^2}\right) >0 \]is not such an irrationality sequence. In particular, any strictly increasing sequence with $\limsup a_{n+1}/a_n <\infty$ is not such an irrationality sequence.

On the other hand, Kova\v{c} and Tao do prove that for any function $F$ with $\lim F(n+1)/F(n)=\infty$ there exists such an irrationality sequence with $a_n\sim F(n)$.

## Site References
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.
- [ErGr80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [KoTa24] Kova\vC, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).

- 22:25 on 18 Dec 2025 - Vjeko_Kovac (reply depth 1):
  This is very nice and quite impressive!
  
  Regarding $a_n=2^n$: You and Aristotle are right. It is sufficient to range $b_n$ over $\{1,2,3,4\}$; I haven't observed this before. The range $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ was simply more convenient, since one only needs a single term from the tail to dominate the "gap" from the preceding term.
  
  Regarding $a_n=2^{2^n}$: Correct, this was not discussed in the paper [KoTa24]; it is a more classical result. Namely, Erdős and Straus in this paper (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1964-19.pdf) from 1964 (Theorem 1) proved the following:
  If a sequence of positive integers $(c_n)$ satisfies\[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{c_n^2}{c_{n+1}}\leq1,\quad
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{LCM(c_1,\ldots,c_n)}{c_{n+1}}<\infty,\quad
  \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{c_n}\in\mathbb{Q}, \]then it has to satisfy the recurrence relation $c_{n+1}=c_n^2-c_n+1$ for sufficiently large indices $n$.
  Now just apply this to $c_n=2^{2^n}+b_n$ for a bounded sequence $(b_n)$, also estimating trivially $LCM(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\leq c_1\cdots c_n$. If the sequence $(c_n)$ satisfied the recurrence relation for large $n$, we would have that $(2b_n-1)2^{2^n}$ is bounded, but $|2b_n-1|\geq1$, so it is not.
  However, it is still impressive that Aristotle figured it all out just by itself!
  
  By the way, yesterday I ran Aristotle for several hours with the same irrationality question but for $a_n=n!$ (entered manually as text), but there was no luck. I believe that this part of the problem is still open.

- 16:05 on 18 Dec 2025 - BorisAlexeev (reply depth 3):
  Here are some of my takes on your questions:
  
  A centralized place where you can ask these questions is the Lean Zulip (https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/), many of them specifically on the topic "Discussion thread for Aristotle API (https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/Discussion.20thread.20for.20Aristotle.20API/with/564270157)". But I think it's fine to ask here -- it's very related to what lots of people are doing here, and you are a respected contributor to the site. :)
  
  It *is* possible to have Aristotle import the FormalConjectures project. You probably have to clone that git repository, and then launch Aristotle from within it. There may be version compatibility issues which plague Lean development in general.
  
  But in this case, it's relatively easy to manually strip down the Lean file to something like this:
  
  import Mathlib
  def IsIrrationalitySequence (a : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ b : ℕ → ℕ, BddAbove (Set.range b) →
   0 ∉ Set.range (a + b) → 0 ∉ Set.range b → Irrational (∑' n, (1 : ℝ) / (a n + b n))
  theorem erdos_264.parts.i : ¬IsIrrationalitySequence (2 ^ ·) := by sorry
  
  The only change really required was to remove "@[category research solved, AMS 11]". In other cases, you might need to copy over a definition from elsewhere in the FormalConjectures repository. It isn't always the easiest thing to find, but maybe an LLM could help?
  
  In this case, this succeeded in about 15 minutes, and you can see the result here (https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fplby%2Flean-proofs%2Frefs%2Fheads%2Fmain%2Fsrc%2Fv4.24.0%2FErdosProblems%2FErdos264b.lean).
  
  Regarding running the real FormalConjectures project in "Lean 4 Web (https://live.lean-lang.org/)": I don't believe that is possible at the moment. I am told that being able to run multiple files online is a feature under development right now.

  But I would wary about the LLM "back-translation". The reason being that LLM and human failure modes are quite similar: both can misread wrong theorem as the "right" theorem if the right formulation makes more sense. - 13:38 on 18 Dec 2025 - Kevin Barreto (reply depth 1):
  FWIW, the statement is formalised correctly. Taken literally, it reads: there exists a sequence $(b_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ taking values in $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and a number $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ s.t. $\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}\frac{1}{2^{k+1}+b_{k+1}}=q$, i.e. so that the sum is rational. The prime notation on $\Sigma'$ in Lean 4 is necessary for denoting an infinite sum. Since the summand here is defined for all $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, it gives what you intend it to be.
  
  Should one want a more human-readable translation of Aristotle's formalisation, see here (https://live.lean-lang.org/#).

- 16:10 on 18 Dec 2025 - BorisAlexeev (reply depth 1):
  Regarding using an LLM to translate back from Lean to English ("de-formalize"): in my experience looking at a bunch of misformalized statements, ChatGPT Pro was able to identify approximately half of the misformalizations. So perhaps there is still noticeable risk in that regard.
  
  However, if you present an LLM with a misformalized statement AND a proof that "cheats" by taking advantage of the misformalization, I have found a very high success rate with the LLM catching that.
  
  The remaining case would be a misformalized statement but with a "proper" proof (for the "real" statement). I'd guess that the LLM would be more likely to miss the misformalization there, because it's accompanied by a proof that doesn't "cheat", but I haven't actually tried this configuration because it hasn't come up.

## Local Computation
Finite compute signal:
 - Computed criterion proxy values:
 - a_n=2^n: stable near 1/3 (strictly positive)
 - a_n=n!: positive values decreasing but clearly nonzero in tested range
 - a_n=2^{2^n}: rapidly tends to 0

 - Finite data aligns with the theorem: exponential-type growth fails the criterion, while doubly-exponential growth remains plausible.

- Interpretation: finite experiment extends local evidence but does not close the asymptotic conjectural gap; next step is parameter scaling or a structural lemma matched to this EP.

## Local Proof Attempts
Target:
Sharpen the obstruction criterion around
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty} a_n^2\sum_{k>n}\frac1{a_k^2},
\]
and characterize exactly when a sequence can be an irrationality sequence.
Step A: Tail-energy normalization
Interpret
\[
E_n:=a_n^2\sum_{k>n}a_k^{-2}
\]
as a local "carry-capacity" parameter in binary-tail approximation arguments.
Step B: Necessity/sufficiency split
Show \(E_n\not\to 0\) blocks irrationality-sequence behavior (known direction);
study converse under mild regularity assumptions.
Step C: Borderline examples
Construct explicit sequences with \(E_n\to0\) and with \(\liminf E_n>0\) to map
sharpness.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a converse theorem: \(E_n\to0\) plus weak regularity implies existence of
infinitely many protected digit windows sufficient for irrationality-sequence
construction.

Proposition DI1 (Obstruction restatement):
If \(\liminf E_n>0\), then the sequence fails the EP-264 irrationality-sequence
property (by Kovač-Tao criterion).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Direct application of the established obstruction theorem.
\(\square\)
Proposition DI2 (Boundary reduction):
The unresolved regime is exactly \(E_n\to0\) without strong monotonic separation
of growth ratios.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Positive-liminf regime is excluded by DI1; extremely fast-growth families are
already known positive examples.
\(\square\)
